newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico sees NAFTA as key savior from crisis.
newsitem.headline: Mexico sees NAFTA as key savior from crisis.

text.p: In Mexico, there is little doubt about the benefits of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA).
Washington on Friday gave the first three years of the free trade pact between the United States, Canada and Mexico a lukewarm appraisal of its benefits for the United States.
But to business leaders, the government and most economists in Mexico, NAFTA has been a saving grace.

"The Mexican authorities should remember that the exporting possibilities gave many national companies the opportunity to continue operating during the country's most difficult economic crisis," Armando Araujo, president of Mexico's National Chambers of Commerce, said Friday.
Free trade facilitated Mexico's 1995 export boom and provided desperately needed income when Mexico was in the throes of economic crisis after the December 1994 peso devaluation.
"Thanks to NAFTA and the guaranteed free trade, it was easier for Mexico to recover through exports from the 1995 crisis," said economist Angel O'Dogherty at GEA consultants in Mexico City.
Exports jumped in 1995 to total $68.4 billion from $53.4 billion in 1994. As consumer spending shriveled, imports sank to $55.4 billion from $58.6 billion.
But as recovery took hold, imports also began to pick up. In 1996, imports grew to $69.4 billion and exports to $81.8 billion.
"The trend will be a continued growth in both imports and exports, so with the recovery Mexico will demand more imports from the United States and Canada," O'Dogherty said.
The United States and Canada are Mexico's main trading partners, absorbing 85 percent of total exports in 1996.
Analysts say NAFTA's benefits will develop over the treaty's initial 15-year lifespan, as most tariffs still in place will gradually disappear by the year 2003.
"There is still a lot to do, but we've seen some important progress, like more efficient customs procedures," said Luis Ramirez, vice chair of the Border Trade Alliance.
"The influence of NAFTA can especially be seen on the (U.S.-Mexico) border with the new infrastructure and technology being implemented," he said.
NAFTA also allows individiual states to negotiate directly rather than through the federal governments, he said, citing cooperation between Arizona and the northern Mexican state of Sonora.
Mexico has been impatient to see trade facilitated even further, and officials are quick to note how the U.S. has dragged its feet in the promised border opening to trucks and courier services.
Anti-dumping tariffs on Mexican items from cement to brooms have also hurt trade relations between the two countries.
"I'm not sure things have progressed to where they should be in the fourth year of the treaty," Ramirez said.
